Whoever comes to shroud me, do not harm Nor question much That subtle wreath of hair, which crowns my arm; The mystery, the sign, you must not touch, For 'tis my outward soul, Viceroy to that, which then to heaven being gone, Will leave this to control And keep these limbs, her provinces, from dissolution. For if the sinewy thread my brain lets fall Through every part Can tie those parts, and make me one of all, Those hairs which upward grew, and strength and art Have from a better brain, Can better do'it; except she meant that I By this should know my pain, As prisoners then are manacled, when they'are condemn'd to die. outputs.L2:
To the person who prepares my body for burial: do not disturb or closely inspect the delicate ring of hair encircling my arm. Leave that secret emblem untouched. It is my soul made visible—the deputy of my true soul, which, after departing for heaven, will leave this behind to govern my limbs, its territories, and preserve them from decay.

If the nerves descending from my brain can bind every part of my body together and make many parts into one person, then these hairs—which grew upward and received their power and design from a superior mind—can perform that task even better. Unless, perhaps, she gave them to me as a sign of the suffering I must endure, just as condemned prisoners are placed in chains before their execution.

Whatever her intention was, let the hair be buried beside me. Because I have died as a martyr to Love, these relics might inspire idolatrous worship if they passed into someone else’s possession. Giving the hair every service a soul can offer was an act of humility; yet there is also a certain defiance in this: since you wanted no part of me, I will carry part of you into the grave.
outputs.L3:
The speaker addresses those who will prepare his body for burial, asking them not to disturb the wreath of hair wrapped around his arm. He regards this lock of his beloved’s hair as more than a keepsake: it is an “outward soul,” capable of preserving his body and holding it together after his true soul has departed. Because the hair comes from the woman he loves, it seems to possess a strength greater than the natural fibers, nerves, and tissues that bind his own limbs.

Yet the speaker remains uncertain about the meaning of this bond. He wonders whether his beloved gave him the hair as a symbol of love and intimacy or as a kind of shackle—an emblem of the suffering, rejection, and condemnation he has endured because of her. In either case, he insists that the wreath must be buried with him. If it remained above ground, others might treat it as a sacred relic and worship it. By taking it into the grave, he also gains a final, dark consolation: although his beloved rejected him in life, part of her will nevertheless accompany him in death.
outputs.L4:
In John Donne’s “The Funeral,” the speaker imagines his own burial and instructs whoever prepares his body not to remove the wreath of his beloved’s hair wrapped around his arm. He treats the bracelet as a sacred mystery, comparing it to a spiritual sign or relic that must not be disturbed. At the same time, he describes the hair through anatomical imagery: it acts like an “outward soul,” binding the body together and preventing it from decaying, just as the soul animates and preserves the living body. Political and legal metaphors deepen this idea, as the hair becomes the soul’s representative or “viceroy” and also a set of “manacles” that continues to hold him captive to love even after death.

The speaker therefore asks to be buried with the hair still encircling his arm. Because he considers himself a martyr to love, the bracelet becomes a relic of his suffering and transforms his grave into something like a sacred shrine. Yet the gesture is not purely devotional. The poem’s conclusion reveals bitterness and defiance: the woman has rejected him and refused to preserve any part of him, so he will take part of her into the grave instead. The lock of hair thus represents both enduring intimacy and possessive revenge. It preserves their connection beyond death, but it also allows the speaker to claim a final victory over the beloved who would not return his love.
